items.question: What can you throw in JavaScript versus C#?
items.answer: JavaScript throw accepts any value — strings, numbers, plain objects, or Error instances. C# requires System.Exception (or derived). Production JavaScript should throw Error or subclasses so err.stack and instanceof work. C# compile-time catch typing is exact; JavaScript needs runtime instanceof checks inside a single catch block.
followUps: Does throw "msg" produce a stack trace?
items.sixtySeconds: JS throws anything; use Error for stack. C# requires Exception types. instanceof in catch. cause like InnerException.

items.question: Explain try, catch, and finally in JavaScript.
items.answer: try wraps risky code. catch runs when throw escapes the try — one catch per try, unlike C# multiple typed catches. finally always executes for that try, whether success, handled catch, or rethrow. return inside try still runs finally first. Avoid throwing inside finally — it can mask the original error.
items.sixtySeconds: try/catch/finally same as C#. One catch. Branch inside. finally always runs. Optional catch { } without variable.

items.question: Why does try { asyncFn(); } catch not work?
items.answer: An async function returns a Promise immediately. The throw or reject happens later on the microtask queue, outside the synchronous try scope. You must await asyncFn() inside try or attach .catch() to the returned promise. This is the JavaScript parallel to forgetting await on a faulting Task in C#.
followUps: How do you fix forEach with async callbacks?
items.sixtySeconds: Async returns Promise. await in try or .catch. forEach ignores promises — use Promise.all.

items.question: What is an unhandled promise rejection?
items.answer: A Promise that rejects with no .catch handler and no awaiting parent try/catch by the time the engine checks. Node emits process unhandledRejection; browsers emit unhandledrejection. Default Node policy may exit the process. Register global handlers for logging and graceful shutdown, but every route and job still needs boundary handling.
items.sixtySeconds: Rejected promise, no handler. Node unhandledRejection. Global handler for logging only. Fix with await or .catch.

items.question: How do you read and improve stack traces in production?
items.answer: Error instances expose stack as a string listing function, file, and line. Log err.stack, not just message. Build tools emit source maps linking minified bundles to TypeScript — upload maps to Sentry or similar. Node --inspect and Chrome DevTools use breakpoints and the debugger statement. Error.captureStackTrace in Node trims constructor frames for custom errors.
followUps: When is stack captured — new Error or throw?
Should source maps be public on CDN?
items.sixtySeconds: Log stack. Source maps to error tracker. debugger for local. captureStackTrace in Node libraries.

items.question: How do C# when filters map to JavaScript?
items.answer: C# catch (HttpRequestException ex) when (ex.StatusCode == TooManyRequests) is a compiler feature. JavaScript has one catch — replicate with if (err instanceof HttpError && err.status === 429). Order multiple conditions from most specific to general inside the same catch, like ordering derived catches in C#.
followUps: Can JavaScript have multiple catch blocks?
items.sixtySeconds: when becomes if inside catch. One catch only. cause maps to InnerException. using maps to try/finally.

items.question: When should you return an error object instead of throwing?
items.answer: For expected outcomes — validation failures, not-found, cache misses — return null, { ok: false, error }, or a Result shape. Reserve throw for programmer bugs, broken invariants, and unrecoverable I/O. Same tradeoff as C# TryParse versus throw on a hot CSV path. Exceptions and stack collection have cost; control flow should stay explicit at API boundaries.
items.sixtySeconds: Return for expected. throw for exceptional. fetch needs res.ok check. Never empty-catch in workers.

items.question: What are common JavaScript error types and when do they occur?
items.answer: Error is the base. TypeError: wrong type or null access. ReferenceError: undeclared variable or temporal dead zone. RangeError: invalid numeric range or stack overflow. SyntaxError: JSON.parse failure or parse errors. Extend Error for domain codes (HttpError with status). Check with instanceof — remember thrown strings are not instanceof Error.
items.sixtySeconds: Error base. TypeError ReferenceError RangeError SyntaxError. Custom extend Error. instanceof not for strings.
